speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is reported to me that over the,radio to-day it was anounced that President Roosevelt has called an international monetary conference for July 1, 1944. subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO ASSURANCE OF PERMANENT EMPLOYMENT TO LABOUR TRANSFERRED TO PACIFIC COAST

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO ASSURANCE OF PERMANENT EMPLOYMENT TO LABOUR TRANSFERRED TO PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: I desire to ask the Minister of Labour a question based on a press dispatch to the effect that national selective service is endeavouring to procure help from other provinces for work in industry on the Pacific coast, with the assurance given them of permanent employment following the end of the war. My question to the minister is: Are such steps being taken, and if so, is the same guarantee being given to all those who have left British Columbia?

subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO ASSURANCE OF PERMANENT EMPLOYMENT TO LABOUR TRANSFERRED TO PACIFIC COAST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not responsible for any statement in the press. There is of course a considerable movement up and down the country under the direction of national selective service; that is inevitable under war conditions and with the civilian labour situation as it is at the moment. I have no knowledge of any guarantee being given as indicated by the hon. member with respect to permanent employment when the war is over.
On the orders of the day:

I wish to direct some questions to the Minister of Labour concerning the lengthy statement given yesterday, as reported in the Canadian press, by Mr. MacNamara, the director of national selective service. No doubt the interview or statement is known to the minister. In the statement it is said that having regard to Canada's position to-day the number in the armed forces or gainfully employed " is just about as high as we can expect to go." Then it goes on to state that certain things are to be done by the department shortly. The questions I would ask the minister are these: In view of the declaration of Mr. MacNamara, do the surveys of the department indicate that there is any hoarding of labour on a large scale? Mr. MacNamara says that measures are to be taken in order to comb out those who have been hoarding labour. What industries are to be affected by further compulsory orders about to be issued, as stated by Mr. MacNamara? Does the statement I quoted a moment ago indicate that it is the intention of the government-
Order. The hon. gentleman has laid the foundation for his questions, and I think he should now put them.

Does that statement indicate that Canada has come to a point about as high as we can expect to go in manpower and that there is to be no change in the matter of call-ups under the National Resources Mobilization Act?

Answering the last question first, no change is contemplated at the moment in the call-ups under the National Resources Mobilization Act. As I indicated when my estimates were before the house, we have a staff who are continually combing the industrial and commercial structure of the country for additional recruits for the army, and we have in motion also a policy of direction, transferring men from less essential to more essential industries. That is going on continuously. It is a day to day administrative policy. As regards the question of additional compulsory transfers, that has not been finalized at the moment, and I do not think I can go further than that at present.

May I ask one
supplementary question? Was Mr. MacNa-

Fresh Fruit-British Columbia
mara stating what is a fact when he said that to-day Canada faces its most acute man-power shortage?
I think that is generally understood. Most grown-up men know that.

subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES
speechtext: I desire to ask a question of the Minister of Finance on a matter which affects fruit growers not only in my riding but in the entire province of British Columbia. I directed a question to the minister some three weeks ago, and again on the 24th of this month, in connection with the picking and disposal of strawberries and raspberries-particularly, at that time, strawberries. Under the present price set-up as established by the board it is impossible for the berry growers to arrange for the picking and salvaging of the crop. I would ask the minister, in view of the seriousness of the situation, and the fact that, with a seasonal crop like this, an immediate or a very early decision is necessary, and the price set by the board makes it uneconomic to pick the crop: First, what provision is being made to have the crop picked and so avoid waste, and, second, will the government give immediate consideration to modifying the administrator's order No. A-1224? The matter is of urgent importance to us in British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. C. ABBOTT (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES
speechtext: Perhaps I might answer that question. Ceiling prices for strawberries were fixed, as my hon. friend has indicated, by administrative order No. A-1224, which was published, I think, on Monday of this week. I understand from my hon. friend that in zone 3, which includes British Columbia, the price is alleged to be not sufficient to cover the cost of production. My hon. friend has asked what the government proposes to do about that: is that correct?

subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES
speechtext: Correct.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES
speechtext:
I received notice of his question a few minutes before coming into the house. I got in touch with the administrator of fruits and was informed that last year, when no ceiling prevailed, the price was higher than the price which has been fixed this year. The price fixed this year is ninety per cent higher than the average for the
years 1938, 1939, 1940 and 1941, and it is felt that it is sufficient to provide an adequate return. That is the only answer I can give to my hon. friend's question, but I shall be glad to bring his further representations to the attention of those concerned.

subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES
speechtext: I would point out that it is of vital importance that we should know when this decision will be given.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRICE CEILING ON BRITISH COLUMBIA STRAWBERRIES AND RASPBERRIES
speechtext: My information is that one of the leading grower organizations of British Columbia was written to to-day in reply to certain representations which had been made setting forth in substance what I have said here, that the ceiling price set is felt to be adequate, and there is no indication at the moment that the price will be changed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, May 25, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war- Mr. Usley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Mines and geology branch-Assistance to provincial governments in construction of transportation facilities into __ strategic mineral, including oil, properties, $75,000.

Mr. Chairman, I would like the minister to give us some information on this vote and tell us why it has been so greatly reduced. This is a very valuable form of assistance that can be given to mineral development. I recall that, in the district I represent, some years ago a prospector found ore in the Zeballos valley so rich he could make wages packing it out on his back over the mountains and along the beds of rivers. Then this government aided by the provincial government gave a considerable sum to make a road up that valley, which not only affected this man's holdings but meant that a' number of others were developed. Inside of a year or more four stamp mills were running in that district. The stamp mills crush the rock. The ore was very rich and the development was very successful. I remember that one mine was turning out $160,000 of gold a month, and as I say four stamp mills were running there in that small area-a situation that hardly could have been found in Canada before. The money that was granted by the dominion government, aided by the provincial government, helped that enormous development to take place. I would like to see that form of assistance continued, but I see that the vote is cut down from $200,000 last year to $75,000 this year. That will not go far in making roads through mountains. Mineral is almost always found in rock, not in a potato field, and rock is generally associated with mountains. To make a road with bridges through the mountains is very expensive. The sum of $75,000 would not make much more than eight or ten miles of mountain road.
3262	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
That would be of very little assistance in promoting any substantial development. Would the minister say why this vote has been cut down so much?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: I think the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is a pertinent one. The amount provided last year was $200,000, and the actual expenditure was $143,000 odd. This vote is to meet requests that may possibly come in from the metals controller for assistance in getting roads built into places where strategic minerals are found. It is not to assist in the ordinary mining development of the country at all. This is a war vote. It may be that this amount will not be required this year; on the other hand, over $75,000 may be required, in which event we would have to find ways and means of getting it somewhere out of the war appropriation. I wish to impress on the committee that while these are estimates they are really very little more than shrewd guesses as to what may be required.
They are something more than tokens, are they not? You are going to spend some money, are you not? And where?

We may not spend any of the money. I explained to the committee yesterday on another vote that these items are included in the estimates to meet possible requests from the metals controller for assistance in developing certain strategic metal mines.
What is a strategic metal?

They are the ones we discussed yesterday, such as tungsten, chromite, molybdenite, manganese if it were found, fluorspar, mercury, and others. It may be that in the course of this year some prospector who has staked a claim in one of the provinces or some company that has a claim staked may come to the metals controller and say, "We have a property that may be valuable in producing tungsten,"-or it may be some other metal required in the war effort-"but we need assistance. We think it is worthy of your examination." The metals^ controller makes an investigation, and if he thinks the property warrants further exploration; we have made provisions for that.
In that case gold would not be a strategic metal?
No.

Will there be a similar vote
in the ordinary estimates?
[M. Neill. 1
I think not this year.
Why not?

I will come to that in a
moment. I was giving an illustration. Suppose the metals controller finds that the property is worth developing but that transportation facilities are required; the amount could be provided out of this vote.
Mr .HANSON (York-Sunbury): Have there been any requests for assistance this year under this vote?
Not up to the present time.

Then of
course this is just an enabling vote which may or may not be used?

Quite so.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury)-:	Has the
government through its own motion or through the metals controller investigated the supplies of strategic metals? I have in mind tungsten. There is in the county which I have the honour to represent, to use the language the hon. member for Que-ens-Lunenburg used recently, a very large deposit of tungsten at Burnt Hill mountain. In the last war some development of that deposit took place; has it been called to -the attention of the authorities in this war, and if so have they done anything about it? I believe that the ore is of very high quality and there is an ample supply of it if it is capable -of reduction. As a matter of fact, the development is one that I think the country ought to undertake. I have always been surprised that the provincial government did not do something about it. I must confess that my knowledge of the property is most superficial, but I -am drawing the attention of the minister to the fact that there is a large deposit of tungsten in the parish of Stanley in the county of York which might be explored and, if it is of good quality, be made accessible-it is not at the moment. It might be an important contributing factor in the present war.

The deposit to which my
hon. friend refers did come to the attention of the metals controller and was examined by him and by the officers of the mines branch of my department. It was one of a great many properties. The decision was not to go ahead with that particular one. I am not in a position at the moment to give the reasons why, but I presume other sources of supply were more readily accessible. The requirements for tungsten at the moment, according to the Department of Munitions and Supply, are not nearly so pressing as they were eighteen

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
months or a year ago. In other words, quite substantial quantities of tungsten have been developed and secured.
In what part of the country?

In various parts. As a matter of fact some of the gold mines, such as Hollinger, find tungsten in with their ores. I am unable to state the quantity, but I know that fairly large quantities come from, that source. Some comes from Nova Scotia and British Columbia.
Would the minister be good enough to have his officers send me what they have in the nature of a report on the Burnt Hill tungsten deposit?

I shall have that sent to my hon. friend, if that will be satisfactory. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni raised the question of assisting in the development of gold producing properties. Commencing in 1936 and for several years thereafter a vote was provided in the estimates of the Department of Mines and Resources for assistance in developing transportation into mining areas. Substantial amounts were spent in conjunction with the provinces in carrying out that work. That vote was dropped at the commencement of the war or shortly after. There has not been the pressing need for gold in the last few years that there has been for many other metals, and so for the moment that has been put more or less aside.
My own opinion is that when the war is over and we come to times of peace the matter of the development of mineral areas, both in base and precious metals, should receive the serious consideration of whatever government is in power. During the depressed thirties there was no single industry that made such a contribution to maintaining the standard of economic wealth we had during those years as the mining industry. It was the one industry that expanded during those years and it continued to expand until the outbreak of war. In connection with base metals there has been a great expansion since the outbreak of war. When the time comes that the story may be told in full, the contribution made by *the metal mines of Canada to the winning of the war will be recognized as a fine contribution indeed. I would hope that in the policies that may be developed when this wretched war is over the type of assistance referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will be taken up again. There is no question of its economic value to the country.

I think the minister is right in reducing this item substantially, because,
as the committee will note, it is to provide transportation facilities for strategic metals development. Last year two large companies, Hollinger in Ontario and Bralorne in British Columbia, were the recipients of the one-third which the government provided in connection with this work and which made up the $142,000 spent at that time.
Apropos of the question asked by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni about gold, the minister hoped that when the war is over any government in power would take up the stimulating of activities in the production of gold. I want to submit to the committee and for the consideration of the minister that we should not wait until the war is over to encourage prospecting for gold and the development of gold mines. I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will probably be with me in that view.
In the first two years of the war under the then minister of finance, the present Minister of National Defence, the gold mining companies of Canada were asked to step up their production, to the highest possible degree. They put in new machinery and did everything to respond to that request. Additional production was needed because the Department of Finance was put to it to find1 gold in order to finance our war needs. Later on, under the liberal treatment that this country received from our neighbours to the south in assisting us in our great munitions production programme and furnishing us under a type of so-called lend-lease with the basic materials we were putting into the munitions we were sending to the mother country and other allies, the need for gold as a means of payment to Washington eased off very materially.
Drafts were made upon the men employed in the gold mines, and I think quite properly. An entirely different programme was adopted by the Department of Finance, and I think quite properly. They said, "We do not need gold with which to pay; we have better relations with our neighbours, and we are financing without the use of gold." It was said that the gold mining industry must bow to the manpower needs of base and strategic metals and other important war industries. Under that state of affairs one company with which I am acquainted has been operating with only twenty-seven per cent of their normal manpower.
Gold production in our country has fallen off, but to my mind that is not so alarming as the fact that the search for new gold mines and new base metals mines, the prospecting which is the very genesis of ultimate production, has also fallen off. That is to be expected, because the prospector is an adven-

turous and courageous man.. I spent ten years of my life among these men in northern Ontario. They have enlisted in overwhelming numbers and after the war they will be back. If the committee agree with me when I say that while we cannot predict the date, we know we shall not lose the war, then my humble submission to the minister is that we should not wait until peace is declared to encourage prospecting again.
Instead of a large item of $142,000 going mainly to two wealthy mining companies to assist in building roads into strategic metals properties I should like to see the minister stimulate the Minister of Finance when he brings down the budget and have provision made this year to provide for the bonusing and encouragement of prospecting. Everyone will tell you that there is a long period from the time a property is first discovered and staked until actual production occurs. Take the Hollinger mine, for instance, which has produced $150,000,000 of gold since it was first discovered. Not if we have only a paper money and nothing behind it.

I do not know what my hon. friend means by that. I hope he is not trying on this item to provoke me into an argument on economic principles. If he thinks we ought to go back to the gold standard, I suggest that he read history. My view is that never again should we return to the gold standard; it would cramp the development of the natural resources of this great country. Perhaps my hon. friend did not mean that. If he did, I should like personally to convert him, if he has a couple of hours or a couple of days to spare.
Or a couple of months.
I should like to show him what is involved.
It will take until after the next election.

There is nothing political in what.I am talking about, and I am sure my hon. friend did not mean to suggest that. The gold industry has been of great value to this country over the past thirty years. Look at the ramifications of the industry, the money which has been spent on wages, machinery, transport, everything which has gone into our economic life. The gold industry of Canada has had a magnificent stabilizing effect upon the economic life of this country. That being so, my only purpose is to urge the minister to say to his colleague or colleagues who bring down our budget: Do not overlook in this present session provisions which will encourage and stimulate the prospector, the man who must come first, before you build your transport or your roads, before you bring your hoists to raise the ore to the surface, before you construct your mills, and remember that four or five years must elapse between the discovery of a property and bringing it into production; so that you must make provision to encourage that branch of the industry.
You are already two years late.

There is some force in what my hon. friend says. I do not know whether he participated last year in the discussion ol this item for the encouragement of prospecting. To my mind the amount was too niggardly a provision, and this country can well afford to increase it. It does not represent very much in the sum total of $5J thousand millions which we spend 'n twelve months.
It has been indicated to me that Canada is not on lend-lease. That of course is true; and I may have created a wrong impression I did not mean to say that we were on lend-lease; I intended to say, on a basis of commercial trading with our neighbours to the south whereby they eased tremendously their demands in the earlier years of the war, before they were allies with us, in requiring us in the earlier years to pay either in kind or in gold. When they entered the war, as they did after Pearl Harbor, their whole economic attitude toward Canada altered very materially; in the past two years they have treated us with a great deal of consideration and a helpfulness which has reduced the need for gold. That is the reason for the change in the attitude of our administration towards gold mining. First it was, " Produce all you can," then, " Ease down and give your men to other industries." Let me therefore correct any suggestion I may have conveyed that we are on a lend-lease basis with the United States. We make a great contribution to them, let it not be forgotten, in nickel and other strategic minerals. Canada's place in the production of strategic metals and the

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
stepping up of that production during these war years is a magnificent war effort of which we may well be proud. Any hon. members who desire to pursue that study will find in our booklet, " Canada at War," a chapter devoted to what we have done in the world picture in the producing of strategic metals.
I have spoken longer than I intended. I merely desire again to impress upon the minister that we should at this very session stimulate prospecting for and the early stages of the production not only of strategic minerals but of gold as well.

The Canadian government can get one-third of the oil, for which it must pay exactly what it cost, plus a fee of 10 per cent. I maintain that the great natural resources of Canada are the birthright of the Canadian people, the birthright of the boys who are fighting on the war-fronts of the world to-day, and when they come back to Canada they expect to take part in the -development of the natural resources of this country in the interests of all the people. In my estimation this is stealing. I have endeavoured to follow the remarks of my hon. friend since he concluded reading the order in council and I am somewhat at a loss to know just what he has in mind. He inquires what the Canadian people will get out of these transactions.
I think that is clearly set out in the order in council and in the regulations forecast in the order in council. How much the Canadian people may get out of it in the end, or how much anyone may get out of it in the end, depends upon factors of -which at the moment we know nothing. If no additional oil were discovered in the Mackenzie river country, I would say that no one is going to get anything out of the development.
Imperial Oil would not be drilling there and proving the field in that case. They have done some drilling and proving there.

highway?
No; that is just the Canol project alone. In laying a pipeline across rugged, mountainous country such as existed between Norman Wells and Whitehorse, transportation facilities had to be provided.
How far is that?
Four hundred miles.

It is more than that; it
is about six hundred miles from Norman Wells to Whitehorse, right over the ridge of mountains. The difficulties were almost insuperable. I ask the committee to bear in mind that this country is in the very far north and it is expensive to provide transportation facilities. All the equipment for drilling, all the pipe, all the supplies needed to maintain the people who were doing the work had to be transported to Waterways by rail. It was then put on boats and taken down the Athabaska river, across the western part of lake Athabaska and down the Slave river to Fitzgerald. At that point every pound of freight had to be taken over a portage of sixteen miles from Fitzgerald to Fort Smith. At Fort Smith the supplies were loaded on barges and boats and taken down to Slave lake and across that body of water, which is rather difficult to navigate under some conditions, to the Mackenzie river. The supplies continued down the Mackenzie to the point where they were taken off the boats to be moved inland over the muskeg to the place where the drilling was done.
I know something of these difficulties because I visited that part of the country in
100-206i
August, 1942, when the work was being carried on with the greatest possible speed. The difficulties to be overcome were tremendous. When they got the pipe and other supplies as far as Norman, which is 1.550 miles from Edmonton by rail and water and portage, they had to be transported out along the pipeline toward Whitehorse. That involved building the type of road that would provide the necessary transportation facilities. As I say, the United States authorities spent an immense amount of money which in the aggregate, as reported to the Truman committee in Washington, amounted to $134,000,000.
The pipeline was a four-inch line. This size was adopted because it was easier to transport than it would have been to transport ten or twelve-inch pipe. This pipe was more readily obtainable because it did not require so much iron and steel which were very pressing needs at that particular time not only in the United States but in Canada. The four-inch pipeline was designed to handle about 3,000 barrels a day.

In winter as well as
in summer time?

Not so much in winter. I have not in mind at the moment what the winter capacity would be, but there is no doubt that the cold weather would interfere with the movement of oil and it would be substantially less. It was estimated that in the event of oil supplies to Alaska being shut off on the Pacific coast this pipeline would provide some of the necessary fuel for the defence of Alaska and northwestern Canada. Canada was vitally interested in seeing this work carried on because, if the Japanese had succeeded in overrunning Alaska and had got into northwestern Canada, we would have had a serious problem on our hands.
Consequently, when the United States made these proposals the Canadian government accepted them. This is all set out in the exchange of notes which were tabled in this house from time to time as soon as they could be. I want to impress upon the committee that this work was purely a defensive measure in our war effort. The picture has changed since. The Japanese are out of the Aleutian islands and the allied nations have increased their strength on the Pacific tremendously. The United States alone has naval forces in the Pacific which are more than a match for Japan. Consequently the danger of an interruption in gasoline supplies by the Aleutians and Alaska being overrun has pretty well disappeared.
The need which led to this project being undertaken no longer existed and it then be-

My government further proposes that the pipeline and the refinery shall remain its property, and shall be operated under contracts with it or by its agents or representatives during the war. It further proposes that at the termination of hostilities the -pipeline and refinery *'*'liall be valued by two valuers, of whom one shall be named by the United States and one

by Canada, with power, if they disagree, to appoint an umpire. The valuation shall be based upon the then commercial value of the pipeline and the refinery, and the Canadian government shall be given the first option to purchase at the amount of the valuation. If the option is not exercised within three months, they may be offered for sale by public tender, *with the amount of the valuation as the reserve priee. Additionally, it is proposed that bo-th governments agree that they will not themselves order or allow the dismantling of either the pipeline or the refinery, nor will they allow any company which purchases them so to do, unless and until approval for dismantlement is recommended by the permanent joint -board on defence.

That has to do only, I believe, with the disposal of the pipeline. It does not deal with the permit for the production and development of oil over that whole area. That is what I was talking about.

I might read a portion of the note which has to do with the question just asked by my hon. friend:
My government,-

faced with -the necessity of obtaining an increased fuel supply without delay, desires to propose the -following project:
That it (a) make surveys and construct a pipeline either by United States army engineers or by contract, of a size sufficient to deliver three thousand barrels of oil daily from Norman Wells, Northwest Territories, Canada to Whitehorse, Yukon Territory, Canada; (b) sign a contract with a Canadian company to drill additional wells, upon its leases obtained under the petroleum and natural gas regulations applicable to dominion lands or upon permits obtained by it under -the oil and gas regulations .covering land in the vicinity of Norman Wells. In the next paragraph it speaks of the refinery. The Imperial Oil company, as was stated earlier, had already drilled wells in the district of Fort Norman-as a matter of- fact they are about forty miles down the river from Fort Norman-and had secured limited quantities of oil. The geologists thought more oil could be secured, and it was on the basis of that possibility that the United States entered into this arrangement. The result was that they provided the equipment-and, I understand, provided the company with the means of carrying on drilling operations. In view of this arrangement, special war-time regulations were issued covering it. If the United States government proposed to advance moneys to the Imperial Oil company, and wells were drilled and oil was found at practically no expense to the Imperial Oil company, the Canadian government-I made the recommendation to the government myself-thought the new regulations should apply. Consequently war-time regulations were promulgated, and under the war-time regulations the govern- . ment were entitled to share equally in whatever assets developed. The war-time regulations were published in the Canada Gazette,
I am told, in January, 1943; at any rate they were tabled.
Is that P.C. 742?

P.C. 742.
We come now to the stage where new arrangements have to be made. I can quite understand the position taken by my hon. friend, and I do not quarrel with him. In the speech he delivered he has not suggested what policy the government should have followed. He criticizes it for giving away vast resources, but I submit that his criticism is not tenable. We have not given the resources away. We have provided for the development of these oil resources on terms which we think are fair and equitable and which protect the public interest. I assume, and perhaps I am wrong, that my hon. friend's contention would be that the government should have gone into this development as a government enterprise. I should like him to say now whether or not that is his contention.

I am a believer in government enterprise in a thing of this kind. The oil as a natural resource belongs to the Canadian people; but since under the war set-up you have decided to go ahead with the development of it, seeing that Imperial Oil is already in the field, and since you are doing something that is essential for the prosecution of the war, we have no quarrel with that. But we do quarrel with the fact that under the order in council the permit to go on with
the development of these resources after the war is continued and the rights for the development, exploration and the taking of oil and selling it, are now in the hands of the Imperial Oil company, which is owned by the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey. What Canada gets out of these resources is too little for the resources that are being handed over. We can estimate Canada's share in the United States government's expenditure, and let Canada take her fair proportion. We have no quarrel with that. But under this arrangement, all the oil development rights, the permits, will continue with the Imperial Oil, and what Canada gets out of one of her great natural resources is not sufficient. I maintain that you have made a bad bargain.

I want to continue the discussion along the line I was taking. I think I understand my hon. friend's position. There are two approaches to this question. He can say that we are not providing for sufficient royalties, or that we are not providing for sufficient revenue to the crown from the development of these resources; or he can take the other line and say that- w-e should not have had an arrangement at all with a private company. That, I gather, is the position he takes, that the government should have developed this as a government enterprise. That is quite in accord with the policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. They have never disguised the fact, and I do not find fault with it. They have a perfect right to advocate that. But what I am trying to get at is what is really in issue here so far as my hon. friend is concerned. It is not the kind of arrangement that we made with the Imperial Oil company but the fact that we made any arrangement at all with them, and that the whole oil development that may ensue in the future in northwestern Canada should be a government-owned, controlled and operated development. I do not think I am presuming too much in saying that.
I did not say you should not have entered into an agreement with them. I say you made a bad bargain with them.

Is

The statement that was read to the house on May 5 and the order in council which the hon. member for Yorkton placed upon Hansard really I do not wish to be critical, but I do not know why my hon. friend did that, because the order in council was tabled and has been available to every member of the committee-
But not to the Canadian people.

Of course, if my friend wishes to send Hansard out to a number of his friends perhaps it is justified on that account. They can read the order in council; but what arrangement was made? First, take the province of Alberta. Alberta operates on oil royalties. Any oil development that I have known anywhere in the world-I will except Russia because at the moment I do not know just what the practice was there-was on the basis of royalties in some cases, plus a ground rental per acre of the areas covered by leases. That royalty in Alberta runs from five to fifteen per cent. The ground rental for the leases, once they are taken up is, I understand, fifty cents an acre and upwards. In the United States the average oil royalties are 12i per cent. Our information is that in south American countries the royalties are the same. In Alaska the United States fixed a royalty rate of 6i per cent on any oil to be found there. These are regulations that were promulgated some considerable time ago.
I mention that background simply to indicate to the committee that the practice generally in all oil-producing companies, not only in Canada, but in other countries, has been to get revenue from the development through the imposition of royalties and ground rentals. That is precisely the principle that we have applied in the Mackenzie river area.
What about the special provision for reducing the royalty in the event of a company not making a profit?

Oh, well, regulations will
provide that royalties may be reduced. After you impose a flat royalty of fifteen per cent and you come to a point in taking the oil from the well that it does not pay to take it out because of the excess of royalty, if you reduce the royalty, say to five per cent, you enable the well to have a longer life, and that, I am advised, is the advantage of a fluctuating rate of royalty. That can be determined by the authorities of whatever government is dealing with the matter, whether provincial or federal.
As regards the set-up in the Mackenzie river country I would ask the committee to keep in mind that it was all set out in the statements which were tabled in the order in council. There are two areas to which I wish to draw particular attention. One is described as the proven area. The proven area consists of approximately five thousand acres; but in that proven area is included the original

'We pay the cost of producing it, plus the management fee of ten per cent, so that we have that. On the oil produced by Imperial Oil which it sells on its own account, it pays a royalty; and it also pays a royalty on the amount coming from the proven area which may go to the United States.

Then, because the Imperial Oil company derived certain advantages under the arrangement it made with the United States, we provided for a scale of royalties which, once licences are secured, go up every five years. For the first five years I think it is 7\ per cent, for the second five years 10 per cent, and thereafter 12i per cent. In addition, once they secure their leases, ground rental on these, properties commences.
There is one other point with which I wish to . deal; that is, the extravagant statement by the hon. member for Yorkton that we were alienating all these resources to the Imperial Oil company. It is expressly stated in the order in council and in the regulations that there shall be a limit to the number and extent of the acreage that can be held by any one company.
Limited to a million acres.

No; it is less than that. In the first place they get a permit to explore; that is the initial step, and that permit may cover two million acres. After a few years that is reduced, and finally it is brought down to the point where they have to say whether or not they are going to take out leases. Once they take out leases the maximum amount they can get is 360,000 acres. So that when my hon. friend states that we have given these vast areas to Imperial Oil, I must assume that he has not closely read-
Yes, I have read it all.

-the proposals that we submitted. When the leases are taken out there is provision for ground rental. That is simply to encourage development.
Then I wish to go one step further and deal with another matter, namely, the arrangement which the government agreed could be made between Imperial Oil and the United States. There is a variation here from the original exchange of notes but, as I stated earlier in my remarks, the United States has spent about $134,000,000 on this project. As a result of that expenditure undoubtedly Canada has

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
secured the development, possibly in a very large, commercial way, of the oil resources of that part of the country, should oil resources be discovered there. So that we provided that the United States should be compensated for the expenditure they have incurred, by saying that under certain conditions they may be entitled to obtain up to sixty million barrels of oil. That oil is for the use of the United States government, for army, navy or air force purposes; they cannot resell that oil, and it has to be taken currently, when production starts. Under the arrangement they have to pay Imperial Oil the cost of bringing the oil to the surface and I think a fee of 20 cents a barrel, which is roughly one-half cent a gallon. There is nothing mysterious about that. Does anyone here think the government should not have taken this step? -Will anyone in this committee claim that after the United States had gone in to develop these resources-true, for their own defence but for the defence of Canada as well-we should say, "No; now your expenditure must go for naught." No one would support that view for a moment. I say that this govermnent, and I think the Canadian people generally, want to maintain good relations with the United States. In our international dealings with that country we want to be fair and we want them to be fair, and within the last few years I think a great deal of progress has been made in that direction.
My hon. friend criticized our arrangement with Imperial Oil on the ground that it is too generous. Let us look at a few of the factors in this situation. Once more I would remind the committee that this oil development is 1,550 miles by rail and water from Edmonton, or almost 1,200 miles in an air line, and that the oil has to be transported from Norman Wells, not very far from the arctic circle, to a market where it can be consumed. What expense is involved in that? The present four-inch pipeline is not a commercial proposition at all. It is estimated that if sufficient quantities of oil were found, at least a ten-inch and probably a twelve-inch pipeline would have to be laid in order to make the proposition commercially practicable. Therefore, what must be done? First, there must be drilling to determine whether there is sufficient oil to warrant the building of a twelve-inch pipeline to seaboard, the cost of which is estimated at $80,000,000. It is further estimated that it will be necessary to discover reserves of 300,000,000 barrels of oil before it would be feasible to build a pipeline that large. So that we had these alternatives. Either the government could go in and risk that amount of money, taking a chance on
marketing the product afterwards, or we could make an arrangement with a private company along the lines indicated in the statement I read to the house, and in the order in council my hon. friend read this afternoon. I do not think there can be any serious criticism of the arrangement the government proposes to make. We want to get the oil resources developed. There has been a good deal of talk in recent months about the depletion of the oil resources of the world. To-day we draw eighty-five per cent of our oil requirements from the United States. What would the United States authorities think of us if Canada were to take the position that we are not going to do anything so far as developing oil is concerned but were going to depend upon the United States to supply us with oil.
We can supply our own needs if we develop the sands in that north country.

The California fields are growing less. Ultimately this development may lead to the supplying of Alaska, British Columbia and the Pacific states with their requirements. We have also a better assurance with this development of securing the needs of eastern Canada for oil. My hon. friend asks; Why do you not take this oil down to the prairies?

I say that we have oil in Canada. Why not develop it?
Mr. CRERAR; Let my hon. friend reflect for a moment what would be involved in his proposal. There would be involved the building of a pipeline to Edmonton, a distance of at least 1,200 miles, and probably 1,400 miles by the route that would have to be followed.

You can take it out to the coast.
Mr. CRERAR; Certainly; that is what we propose to do under this arrangement. But Standard Oil controls it.
I must ask the hon. member for Yorkton to address the Chair if he wishes to speak.

There is just one other point I would mention. Under these proposals the regulations will apply generally. There are no reservations for Imperial Oil, other than the areas they now hold and referred to in the order in council. Any person who has the capital and wishes to go in there and take the risk can go in there and prospect and develop, but he cannot secure in excess of the amount that I mentioned a moment ago.

optimistic about the C.C.F chances than most people.

It may interest
. the committee to know that on the first of this month I took part in the ceremony of the official opening of the oil refinery at Whitehorse to which the oil which has been discussed this afternoon is being piped for refining. I remember well when the discovery of oil in the vicinity of Fort Norman was made thirty years ago. At that time I happened to be Commissioner of the Yukon, and I know that gold miners from the Yukon valley made their way across the divide into the Mackenzie valley and staked out oil leases on that discovery. For the most part they snowshoed

out of the valley of the Yukon over the watershed and down into the Mackenzie, where they staked out their leases.
When I returned to Canada after the war and came here as a member of parliament, the holders of these oil rights, not having capital to develop them themselves and not being able to interest capital in their development, put it up to me to deal with the government of that day to extend the terms of their leases so that they could continue to hold them without having to do the development work and make the substantial expenditure called for by the terms of the leases. The government extended the time. But finally the time came when they would no longer allow that to go on. They were reasonable enough. It had to come to an end some time.
The Imperial Oil company, which had acquired some of the oil reserves, because of their isolation and distance from the market, had to cap the three wells they had, and the wells lay there dormant until mine, development began at Great Bear lake and at Yellowknife, and then a little oil was used.
Then came Pearl Harbor and the Americans had to have oil. They thought the Japanese might take possession of the coast of Alaska and the coast of British Columbia. Oil could not be got to Alaska by tankers because the submarines were attending to that. So that the United States came in, and they have spent $134,000,000 in exploring those oil resources for Canada. Fortunately the exigencies of war never made that oil necessary for war purposes. But the Americans put in a four-inch pipeline from Norman Wells to Whitehorse and extended it from Whitehorse to Fairbanks, and from Whitehorse to the coast, to Skagway, Alaska. As the minister said, that four-inch pipeline is too small for a commercial undertaking.
I only hope that the development of the wells at Norman will be sufficiently extensive to make it a successful commercial undertaking. I for one would not approve the Canadian government, going in there and spending anything like $134,000,000 in exploring that oil deposit as the United States have done. We had the experience not long ago of the government of British Columbia spending a huge amount of public money on drilling in the Peace River block. They lost it all; they have no oil. I do not think public money should be gambled in that way.
When I first read the agreement and heard the minister give his explanation of it a * month or so ago I felt that the terms granted to Imperial Oil were somewhat too generous. When you take into account the risks that

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
that company has taken, similar to what the United States has taken, and the returns that are bound to accrue to Canada if the gamble is a success, then I think we should compliment the government on the agreement they made.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon and express my appreciation of the excellent manner in which he delivered them. I wish also to dissent and join issue with the remarks of the hon. member for Yorkton. I do not think Imperial Oil has been given any undue advantage under this order in council. I am not particularly interested in theories or in the relative merits of public or private ownership, but I am interested in the results that are obtained. I want to see action in the north country; I want to see developments. I want to see this government give every encouragement to Imperial Oil and to any other oil company that wishes to go into that country. I want to see this government give every encouragement to every mining company, every prospector, every fisherman, every farmer and every other corporation or person who want to help to develop that Mackenzie river valley.
I am not worried about Imperial Oil making any undue profit or of retaining that profit after they have paid income tax. Any profit they may be able to make will be small compared with the benefits that will accrue to Canada as a whole from this development. There are not only oil resources to be developed; there are minerals in the Great Slave and Great Bear lakes areas; there is fishing; there is agriculture, and there are many other types of development that can be carried on. A balanced and orderly development of these resources will mean the production of new wealth and an increase in the national income of Canada.
There will be provided opportunities for thousands of Canadians, particularly for our returned men. These are the things in which I am interested. I want to see a real development in that north country. I particularly want to see that development because it will mean the development of the northern part of the constituency of Peace River. It means also that there will be created in the great north land a market for the produce of the Peace river country.
My hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party are claiming that Imperial Oil is a monopoly. I do not like monopolies. I do not like private monopolies, nor do I like public monopolies. I know I would not like the kind of monopoly we would have if my hon. friends were in power.

While I dislike monopolies, it is not an obsession with me. Monopolies seem to be an absolute obsession with my hon. friends, and yet at the same time they admire monopolies. They contend that monopolies make huge profits, but I cannot see that they do. I do not think monopolies are very efficient. Like most giants they grow slow and sluggish, whether they are private or public monopolies. I certainly do not fear monopolies because as long as we have a free parliament we can deal with them. But what we would not be able to deal with is the type of monopoly my hon. friends of the C.C.F. would create if they were in power.
Some weeks ago we dealt with what might be termed a monopoly in the form of Canadian Pacific Air Lines. We passed legislation which practically wiped that company out of existence and there was not one voice in this house raised in protest. We can deal with monopolies. I think there is some indication that monopolies are rather defenseless when they come up against public opinion.
My criticism is not that the department is doing too much for Imperial Oil; it is that the department is not doing enough for the development of the north country. The department is too much inclined to pay attention to such carping criticism as we have heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Yorkton. The greatest blow that the north country ever received in the past, the greatest handicap it had to overcome was such carping criticism. Probably it will be the greatest handicap the north country will have to face in the future.
Somebody has mentioned the possibility of a pipeline from Fort Norman to the south. In 1921 a private bill was submitted to the Alberta legislature to incorporate the Imperial Pipeline company. In 1920 Imperial Oil brought in a producing well at Fort Norman and they submitted this bill to permit the building of a pipeline south through Alberta. What happened? A tremendous filibuster was opened up and arguments much along the lines of those used by my hon. friends were advanced. It was said that Imperial Oil was a monopoly and the filibuster was kept up from some time in February until late in April. Not only that, but attacks against the bill were carried on throughout the province and in the press.
By whom?

By people with exactly the same attitude of mind as my hon. friend, men who would rather adopt a policy of cutting off their noses to spite their faces than to see a development carried on by what they termed

a monopoly. On the last day of the session the premier of Alberta read a telegram which he had received from Mr. Herbert Greenfield, president of the United Farmers of Alberta, protesting emphatically against the passing of the bill and demanding that it be withdrawn. The bill was withdrawn under this pressure and the house rose the next day.
A few weeks later the government went to the country and were defeated. A U.F.A. government came into power, headed by the same Herbert Greenfield. Toward the end of its career that government was affiliated with the C.C.F. movement, and in 1935 went to the country calling itself a C.C.F. government.
