Mr. Chairman, in my remarks before six o'clock I think I made it clear that I am not especially interested in any academic debate on the relative merits of public and private enterprise. I stated that I was very much interested in the development of all the great and varied resources of the north land, and would favour even more generous treatment, not only of the Imperial Oil company but of every corporation and every individual prepared to play a part in the development of any of those resources; and that I deplored'the reactionary ideas and the defeatist philosophy of the hon. member for Yorkton and his friends. I pointed out that the attitude of the hon. member and those who think like him is the greatest handicap that the north country has had and has to overcome, and I went on to show how a similar attitude had held up the development of the oil resources of that great land in times gone by. I pointed out that in 1921, when the bill to incorporate the Imperial Pipelines company was before the Alberta legislature as a private measure, it was defeated by a filibuster directed largely by men who thought as the hon. member for Yorkton thinks, and by pressure from outside the house of those who held similar ideas.
I wish to make only a very few further remarks regarding that debate in the Alberta legislature some twenty years ago. During the course of that debate the late Hon. J. R. Boyle

pointed out what the obstructionist tactics would result in, and Mr. Boyle wanted to know if the Imperial Oil company were to be told that they were free to spend vast sums of money in exploration work but that if oil was found they were not to pipe it out. That is exactly the attitude which was taken in Alberta; the Imperial Oil company were in effect called upon to spend their millions on exploration work, but if they did find oil they were not to be allowed to pipe it out. Probably a more significant statement was made during the course of that debate by Mr. R. B. Eaton, one of the members. Mr. Eaton stated that " the question of oil development should be carefully taken into account, because the oil resources of the north might easily be diverted to British Columbia if Alberta placed impossible barriers in the way of companies planning development." Back in 1921 Alberta did place impossible barriers in the way of a pipeline from the Fort Norman field to Alberta, and you see the results to-day. That oil is not being diverted, as Mr. Eaton thought it might be, to British Columbia, but it is being diverted to the Yukon, and to Skagway in the United States territory. That is a penalty the provincial government of Alberta paid for giving attention to the carping criticism of men who in Alberta at that time thought and uttered the thoughts which the hon. member for Yorkton has uttered this afternoon.
As mentioned, in 1921 the government then in office was defeated and a U.F.A. government came into power. That government was in power from 1921 to 1935, and during its whole term of office very little encouragement was given to the development of the north land, particularly that part of the north land which lies in the Peace River constituency north of the Peace river. The development of that area, particularly the fertile territory north of the river in the district of Fort Vermilion, was retarded, and retarded deliberately. I do not make that statement concerning the late U.F.A. government because it was a United Farmers of Alberta government or because its philosophy was largely that of my friends of the C.C.F. To a less degree the same thing must be said of the present Social Credit government of Alberta, and I would ask my hon. friends of the Social Credit party not to take offence, because I would say the same thing largely of the government I support. I do not believe that either the old U.F.A. government of Alberta, the present Social Credit government of Alberta, or any federal government of Canada has ever given the encouragement which should have been given to the development of that north land. I admit that the present government has done

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
some things, but it has done far too little. It has been content more or less to make gestures. I am not unmindful that the Department of Mines and Resources has done a good work in regard to geological surveys. I am not unmindful that an important forward step was taken when the air fields in the Mackenzie river valley were taken over by the government. I am not unmindful of the good which will result from the civil aviation policy announced some weeks ago by this government respecting the opening up of that north land. I am not unmindful of the assistance which was given by the dominion and provincial governments toward the construction of the winter road from Grimshaw to the north in order to open up that territory. But I still say that no government, provincial or federal, has done more than a small part of what should have been done to open up that empire of the north.
I do not ask that governments should do a great deal, but I ask that they should do things which only governments can do, and these they have not done. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre lived in the Peace river country he would not be so complimentary to public ownership, its performances and its possibilities. All governments have failed in their duty to encourage this development.

The Canadian
Pacific Railway company has done a good job.
.Mr. SISSONS: The Canadian Pacific Railway company did no job toward the development of the north country, nor did the Canadian National Railways. I shall have something to say about that a little later.
I believe that a great part of the development of the north country in the future as in the past will be brought about by men and not by governments. Men with the blood of the pioneers have brought about the present development of the agricultural lands of the Fort Vermilion district, where there are now 3,000 settlers, still 250 miles beyond the railway. I am not unmindful of those mining pioneers who have pioneered in the lake Atha-baska, the Great Slave lake and the Great Bear lake districts. I am not unmindful of the pioneer work done by the Imperial Oil company. I am not unmindful of those young pioneering pilots who blazed air trails through all the north land. These are the men who have brought about our present development. It will be men of that type who will bring about the great development of that country in the future. But there are some things which governments and only governments can do, and
it is these things which I want the government to do. Years ago the Alberta government should have built a highway from Grimshaw up through that fertile Fort Vermilion country. That has not been done. Our own federal government should do certain things. They should give greater assistance to those who wish to play a part in the development of the north land, much greater assistance than they are giving to the Imperial Oil company. They should provide markets for the produce which that vast country can provide. Especially, they should provide railway transportation for that north country.
The hon. member for St. Paul's mentioned a moment ago the Canadian Pacific Railway company, but I wish to deal for a moment with the Canadian National Railways. That whole northland was the territory of the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National had that territory for years and never developed it, and it allowed the Canadian Pacific to come in and take over, under lease, the Northern Alberta railway. The Canadian Pacific did nothing toward developing that territory. Later the Canadian Pacific Railway company and the Canadian National Railways jointly purchased the Northern Alberta railway and came to this parliament and had passed the Northern Alberta Railway Act which provided among other powers that a branch line should be constructed from Grimshaw to the northern boundary of the province. That is a line which would have opened up the Mackenzie river valley. That was in 1929 and not one foot of the line has been built since.
Now we find both the Canadian Pacific Railway company and the Canadian National Railways, joint owners of the road, coming forward with this proposition, that they should not be asked to build one mile of railway into any part of that north country until there has been developed sufficient traffic that it can pay a profit from the commencement. That is the attitude of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. Now I am going to ask the government to do several things, but one thing in particular I do ask is that they go to the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway company and put the situation up to them in this way: "Either you people do your duty and develop that north country, giving it the transportation which it was understood you would give it when this parliament passed the Northern Alberta Railway Act in 1929, or we shall ask parliament to repeal that act and hand the assets of the Northern Alberta railway over
3282	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
to someone who has a wider vision and who is prepared [DOT] to play the necessary part in the development of that north country."
All I ask is that this government and the provincial government have vision when it comes to the development of that north land, and particularly that this government pay no attention to such carping criticism as has been uttered this afternoon by the hon. member for Yorkton. Let the government pay no attention to such things but branch out on a programme of development for that whole north land which will repay itself many times over. Branch out on a programme of development which will produce new wealth, add to the national income of Canada and bring a greater measure of prosperity to Canadians in that area and in all parts of Canada.
That is what I ask. I also ask for even a larger measure of support than is contemplated in the vote. Let us help all those who would have a part in that northern development.

We have had two really interesting addresses to-day, one of them delivered by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Sissons). While most of what) he has said in the last half of his remarks has nothing whatever to do with the vote, I endorse every word he said about the north country and I agree with him in that regard. The other address was given by the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Black), and it was refreshing to hear first hand information from that hon. gentleman, who told the story of the commencement of this oil business. I wish someone had mentioned the beginner, the real pioneer, the man who more perhaps than any one else had to do with what is now called the Canol project or, as it should be rightly called, the oil development fifty miles down the Mackenzie river from Fort Norman. That gentleman is Colonel James K. Cornwall of Edmonton, one of the real pioneers of the great northwest, from whom I have personally learned great deal and with whom I have had much correspondence with reference to the north on the occasion of various preparations for trips to that country.
I believe it was about 1912, or in fact some years prior to the great war, and particularly when the Turner valley was being opened, that, according to information given me by Colonel Cornwall himself, he had a conversation with a promoter who spoke to him with reference to investing in Turner valley oil. He said, if I remember, to the promoter, "I am not going to invest any money in Turner valley oil because there is more oil in Mackenzie river area than anywhere else I have had to do with."
Apparently, following that, the prospectors to whom the hon. member for the Yukon referred were the first into that country; and as that hon. member said, they took up claims. These claims were later purchased by the Northwest company, a very fitting name, a subsidiary of Imperial Oil, which itself is a subsidiary of Standard Oil of New Jersey. In reference to the vote itself, I wish to support the minister in one stand he is taking, as referred to in the agreement, with which I presume he has had something to do if he is not largely responsible for it, namely, that the oil shall be developed if possible by private enterprise. I personally am wholly opposed to the government going into any business on that scale.
I agree with the department's proposal to assist in the development of the oil by financial assistance to private concerns. In that way we shall get a much better development; it will cost the country much less, and moreover there will be far more, returns if it is developed privately, with the support of the government. But if the government itself proposes to develop the oil we shall get the same exhibition that we have had in most businesses operated by governments. I am not blaming this government alone; that goes for any government. No government can operate business with anything like the same economy as a private firm can.
What does the agreement call for? All I want to be certain of is that Canadian interests are protected. I have read the agreement, and at the moment I do not see that I can suggest any improvement. Someone would have to show me where it could be improved from the point of view of the country. If the agreement recommended that the government itself should develop the oil resources up there I would be opposed to that; but the agreement does not say that. Furthermore, I like the attitude of the minister toward Imperial Oil. I cannot understand the attitude of people, who know little about business, who nevertheless denounce business. We hear it denounced here and it is easy for those who have not had experience in big business to engage in these denunciations. But big business has done a great deal for the whole country.
As regards Imperial Oil, what happened? They puehased the right from the Northwest company to the claims and then commenced to invest money there. They drilled or made attempts to drill many holes in that area to find oil, but they did not find it at every place they drilled. The Minister of Munitions and Supply probably knows more about

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
this than anybody else, but I believe that at the outbreak of war there were three wells in existence, and they were not working at that time. They had been in operation during the time of the development of the radium mine on the east end of Great Bear lake and during the developments at Yellowknife and the other gold centres north and east of Yellowknife. There were seven mines in that area altogether, but that development was not sufficient to take up the oil that could be produced from the three wells, so that I believe they were shut down. If my memory serves me rightly they produced about 24,000 barrels of oil in the last year they operated.
Following the United States entering the war and the necessity of producing oil, which was *explained by the minister, and I do not intend to repeat it now, increased production took place at Fort Norman. An additional number of wells were drilled. I believe that before the war five were drilled that could produce oil .and since that time the number has increased to twenty-three. Some twenty-six wells have been drilled and I believe that the capacity of the twenty-three is about 8,500 barrels a day. That is a considerable surplus over the possible capacity of the pipeline which was built from Fort Norman to Yellowknife, a distance of some 620 miles. When the pipeline was first laid out it was not to be as long as that, but they found that they had to go down the river a piece, and the total length from Fort Norman to Yellowknife is 620 miles.
If my hon. friend will permit me a moment, the present production of the existing wells at normal flow is about 3,900 barrels a day and not 8,000 barrels as my hon. friend says.

I said that the capacity was 8,500 barrels a day. I do not think I said that they were producing 8,500 barrels a day, but the information I have from the engineers is that the capacity is about that. I do not know whether that is right or not, but in any event the production of 3,900' barrels a day is more than the capacity of the pipeline, which is 3,000 barrels a day.
Personally I want to be assured that after the war, when this agreement has been carried into effect, those who have to do with taking over the equipment will be qualified to understand the length of life of pipe, if the pipe is steel, or iron. If the four-inch pipe is not an iron pipe the length of its life is limited, relatively speaking, to a brief space of years. It will rust and go out if it is steel pipe. If it is a wrought iron pipe, of course it will last much longer. Therefore, in taking over the plant after the war the great consideration with me as to what should be paid for it is,
what is the pipe made out of? This pipe crosses damp country; much of it was laid in muskeg; a lot of it was laid during the winter time on ice, which has since become covered with water. It was perhaps laid on props or supports of some kind, that is a consideration. Therefore the length of the life of the pipeline would be the determining factor with me if I had anything to do with passing comment on what should be paid for the plant after the war; but that will have to wait until then.
There is nothing more I wish to say in reference to this matter. There is nothing we can do about it. We should all be unanimous on the necessity of producing oil in the country, if it can be produced. I was talking to a man recently who told me that the distance from Norman to Aklavik would be some 500 to 600 miles. That would not be a long pipeline. This gentleman told me that after the war-and plans are being made for it now-it was intended to run a line of tankers through the Bering strait and around Alaska to Aklavik with the expectation that at that time the Norman wells will have developed to such an extent that it would be worth while running a pipeline of 500 or 600 miles from Norman wells, to tankers there. If that is what is going to happen then the oil could go down to Vancouver and be refined there, which would help to make the great city of Vancouver much larger than it is to-day.
Along with the hon. member for Peace River I see vast developments in that north country and the whole northwest country. At the moment I am thinking of going away to the far north again this coming summer with a view to seeing with my own eyes what can be done. I agree with what the minister and others have said, namely, that a large part of the future of this country depends on the opening up of the whole northwest country, the Northwest Territories and the northern half of the three prairie provinces, if we can awaken out of our lethargy. I am not blaming anyone for it. I like to keep these things out of the narrow' sphere of politics which has done more to retard progress in Canada than anything else. If w'e can get beyond that, up on the higher plane of patriotic development and fervour and all work together irrespective of party lines for the development of this country after the war there would not be any need for any unemployed men or women.	[DOT]
I hope that when the war is over and the possibilities of this territory are realized we shall do something. In that connection I think of Vilhjalmur Stefansson, who explored this northwest country and said that in his

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
opinion there is more oil around Fort Norman than in any other flowing wells in Canada. If that is the case Canada should develop it, along with the Athabaska tar sands which I am not going to go back on. In my opinion they could be worked jointly, and Canada could be placed on a self-sustaining basis, so far as oil is concerned.
As the minister said to-day, and as I said last night, we import eighty-seven per cent of our oil requirements. Let us try to get out of that. Do not let us quibble over the advocacy of the hon. member for Yorkton. I think about as much of his plan as the hon. member for Peace River does.
Why not develop our own oil?

The difference between my hon. friend and myself is this: I have been a producer for many years. I have been in big business. I have operated big business and have had to do with giving employment to many thousands of people in the aggregate. I doubt if my hon. friend ever gave a job to a man in his life other than to cut the grass on his front lawn or such like.
The people of Canada felt the results of big business, too, from 1930 to 1939.

I get absolutely tired of listening to men who know little or nothing about production and less about giving employment. I like to talk to men who have done things, and I like to listen to them. I do not care to waste my time listening to men who have never done anything that I know of or ever read of or ever heard of toward production in this country. If we can get the real men of this country together, the men who know and the men who do things like the Minister of Munitions and Supply we shall be doing something. The minister is on the opposite side of the house, but I cannot get down on such a small plane as not to recognize a man's ability because he happens to be on the other side of the house. My hon. friend the Minister of Munitions and Supply can do a big job. I said last night in the minister's absence that if he had only been at Fort McMurray last year and the year before he would have produced oil. I have that much confidence in him. I do not want him to say I am wrong.
Let us get on a higher plane as we think of this great country, with more resources than any other nation in the world. We have more than ninety per cent of the world's asbestos in Quebec, more than ninety per cent of the world's nickel in Ontario, andmore than ninety per cent of the world's oil in Alberta and the
	_	; [JT[
northern country. If we do not awake from our sleep, Mr. Chairman, and recognize what God has given us to develop, some other country may come in and take it away from us. I say all power to anyone who can advance a plan to develop this country, for the good of the country and to create employment. In conclusion, I repeat that I hope the minister will stick to the private production of oil, not only in the northwest but at Fort McMurray, after the war.

I am not going to waste the time of the committee by replying to the barrage of words that were thrown at us this afternoon. If we look at the condition of want that has prevailed in this country for seventy-five years; if we remember that the only time we have enjoyed decent wages for labour and parity prices for farmers has been in time of war; if we recognize the record of the gentlemen who have been in power in this country since it has been a country, the wealthiest land in the world, with only eleven million people living in it, I think all that is sufficient answer to those who have been advocating the continuance of things as they were in the past. We have opened up western Canada and British Columbia; what has it meant to the welfare of the Canadian people? What did it mean in 1930 to 1939?
Who opened it up? Not you.
Big business opened it up, and what did the workers get out of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The pioneers opened it.
And where are the pioneers to-day?
We have lived better than any other people in the world.

With a billion dollars spent on relief and forty per cent of our young men unable to earn a living.
' The CHAIRMAN: Order. We are discussing a special item in connection with the Canol project. I do not want to curtail discussion, but I do not believe hon. members will tolerate repetition ad nauseam, and I am going to try to confine the discussion from now on to the item under consideration.
I thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, and I shall abide by your ruling. Later on I hope you will see that I am given an opportunity to reply to those statements, if I may not do so now.

That is the C.C.F. again.

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
I suppose I am not allowed to reply to these interjections thrown at me. You maintain order on one side, but I am not allowed to reply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must appeal to the committee in reference to the statement made by the hon. member. I wish he would withdraw his remark. I try to be fair and I believe I have been fair to the hon. member for Yorkton and all other hon. members of the committee. I have always tried to be impartial, but I repeat that in the general discussion which took place this afternoon and the early part of this evening all parties expressed their viewpoints, and I am going to keep hon. members within the confines of the item now under consideration.

I am very sorry if I have cast any reflection upon the Chair, and I withdraw my remark. This afternoon the minister stated that the arrangements made under this agreement would not prevent any other company or companies from taking part in that development. I should like to draw his attention to one of the notes exchanged between the governments of Canada and the United States. This note is dated January 18, 1943, and was written by Mr. Keenleyside in reply to a note from the United States government dated December 28, 1942. The last paragraph reads:
It would facilitate the drafting of regulations if the United States authorities would indicate more definitely the particular districts, within the very large area described in your note No. 818, paragraph 2, which seem to be the most promising. These districts could then be reserved for exploration by nominees of the United States government.
Apparently there was a reservation for the government of the United States. The minister stated that no measures would be taken to prevent other companies from developing this region, but from this note it would appear otherwise.

The effect of the two notes to which my hon. friend has referred is that at the request of the United States government a certain area was reserved for exploration. The right to go out and search for oil structures; the right to examine territory to see if there are favourable conditions for oil, would not confer any right upon them to exploit the property. That was not put under their control at all. The only thing the United States government were interested in was getting a sufficient supply of oil. They thought they might require up to 20,000 barrels a day. No private companies were going in at that time and searching for oil structures. My officers will correct me if I am wrong, but
the United States simply said, "Will you reserve a certain area, where we can send our geologists to see if we can find favourable structures," and that is all that was done. It did not give the United States government any right to preempt any territory, and that is where my hon. friend has misunderstood the meaning of the exchange of notes. No monopoly was conferred upon the United States government or anyone else under these regulations. I stated this afternoon that under the terms of the proposed regulations Imperial Oil may get the right to explore an area of perhaps 2,000,000 acres, but over a period of years that must be reduced to 350,000 acres.
I think it is 1,000.000 acres under the agreement.

Yes, but eventually it
comes down to 350,000 acres. When oil may be found anywhere over 100,000,000 acres I do not think you are setting up a monopoly if you lay down regulations under which eventually a company, after it has examined a certain area, may operate in 350,000 acres; really my imagination is not quite keen enough to bring me to the conclusion that this is conferring a monopoly on the company. I am sure my hon. friend is quite sincere and in earnest in the criticism he is offering, but I suggest that he has not appreciated the full meaning of the regulations and the exchange of notes.

I do not think there
is any doubt about that.

I should like the minister to explain two or three features in connection with this northern development. The first explanation is the general policy of the government with regard to the development of our north country. Last evening I mentioned the developments that have taken place in Siberia, and this evening the hon. member for Peace River stressed the need for great developments in northern Canada. I wish the minister would give us some idea of what the government have in mind as a general policy for developing northern Canada. I am convinced, as I think perhaps most hon. members are, that there are great prospects for development in that part of the country.
The other matter about which I should like a further explanation has to do with the ways in which another company or other companies or private individuals or syndicates will be able to go 4n and develop oil wells in this territory. The minister dealt with that in part, earlier in the debate. There seems to be no doubt that this Mackenzie river oil field is the finest in Canada. The Minister of
3283	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
Munitions and Supply said last year that it was a very fine field, and I have here the March 13 issue of the publication known as The Oil Weekly, published in Houston, Texas, in which there is a long article by Doctor *G. S. Hume, geologist for the oil controller for Canada. The article is headed: "Mac-kenize River Basin Best Opportunity for Oil in Canada." The minister will correct me if I am wrong, or if this statement is wrong. Doctor Hume, in his article, states this at page 26:
The Mackenzie river valley, comprising 150,000 .square miles and extending westward into the Wind river basin of the Yukon, the most promising oil territory in Canada, recently has been brought to the attention of the public by the Canol project, which includes the development of a field that was discovered more than twenty years ago by Imperial Oil company.
Then, further down on the same page we find this:
Doctor O. B. Hopkins of Imperial Oil has stated that a major oil field comparable with a major oil field in the United States has been found and that the area has been proven much larger and more productive than originally anticipated.
So that we apparently have something worth while-very much worth while-in this Mackenzie river oil field.
It just so happens that in the same magazine appears an editorial pointing out the great opportunities for United States oil interests to undertake development in Canada. It [DOT]says, after describing the possibilities in [DOT]Canada:
All these factors will result in relatively large representation dn this "foreign" development by smaller American oil companies, independent [DOT]operators, and geophysical, drilling, and other service companies.
I think we should be sure that these other [DOT]operators will have a reasonable chance to [DOT]succeed in the Mackenzie river field. Frankly, I am not convinced that that is the case at present, under the law as it now stands in Canada. I realize that the Canol project was undertaken as a war emergency measure. But the order in council of January 28, 1943, under which Canada gave approval to that [DOT]development, P.C. 742, contains this paragraph:
1. A permit for a location on lands lying within a radius of 50 miles from Discovery Well .of Northwest Company Limited-
Which, I understand, was a subsidiary of the Imperial Oil company.
-situated about 45 miles north of Fort Norman on the Mackenzie river, conveying the exclusive right to prospect and drill for, to produce and dispose of oil and gas thereon may be granted by the minister to any corporation or to any person eighteen years of age or over for the duration of the present war, provided however -that no person shall enter the area to which

these regulations apply for the purpose of prospecting for oil and staking a location without first obtaining from the minister a preliminary authority so to do.
I believe under that power the Imperial Oil company was given an exclusive right, not only to explore, and not only to prospect but also to drill for, produce and dispose of oil.
Then, later on, namely on March 26, 1943, order in council P.C. 2447 was passed. This order in council extended the territory from a territory within the radius of fifty miles of the old well, to include the whole of the Yukon territory and, the minister will correct me if I am wrong, also all of the district of Mackenzie west of a line drawn roughly seventy-five miles east of the Mackenzie river. I presume the Imperial Oil company got the same exclusive rights with regard to that territory, or as much of it as they wanted. Presumably no other company or individual was given any permit.
Then, this year order in council P.C. 2904 of April 27, 1944, which was read into Hansard this afternoon was passed. It certainly gives the Imperial Oil company every advantage. For example, as I read it, in any part of the field that has been proven; in other words, any part where producing wells have been bored, the Imperial Oil company again has exclusive rights. That is, it will have the whole of the proven field. I may be wrong in that, but the minister will correct me if I am.
Who proved it? Was it not the Imperial Oil company that proved the field?

For example, section 1 (a) of this order in council states:
In respect of the proven field (a) the area to be developed as a unit operation by the company . . .
I take it that means that the Imperial Oil company have exclusive rights to the oil in the whole of the proven field. They also have rights to the balance of about 140,000 acres, over which they have permits. And they have the right to substitute for any part of that
140,000	acres a similar territory, or a like amount of ground in the other part of the whole area.
That is not correct.
I would ask the minister to correct me, because I am simply asking for information.
Well, that is not correct.

It looks to me as though any other company or any other operator is

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
almost doomed to failure in that field, under present conditions, unless some way can be found of giving help to them. I would ask the minister to give us some further explanation respecting that feature of the development, because I do not think it is right to give the Imperial Oil company a monopoly in this Mackenzie river oil district. That may not be the situation, but certainly it is not right that they should have a monopoly. If we can develop that country as Russia has developed part of Siberia there may be 100,000 or 200,000 people there eventually. And it is far more likely to receive proper development if we do not permit any one company to have a monopoly in the area.
The third feature about which I should like to have an explanation is the government's policy with regard to the United States. Just a few weeks ago either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Munitions and Supply, I am not sure which, explained to the house that the government proposed to buy out certain .American interests in the north. That is, we were to repay the money that had been spent in developing air fields, and in buying land and erecting buildings. The Canadian government is buying the United States government *out in respect of those operations, so that such developments will be purely Canadian-owned.
As I understand it, that is not being done with either the Alaska highway or the Canol project. I would ask the minister to say just what the plan is with regard to the relation-.ship between Canada and the United States in respect of the Alaska highway and the *Canol project. He admitted 1o-day that the United States army is to operate the pipeline ifrom Norman to Whitehorse, and presumably is also to operate the refinery at Whitehorse, * and the pipeline from Skagway to Whitehorse. But we should know just what arrangements there are between the two governments in [DOT]respect of these two projects, and whether there are any other developments in northern Canada in which the United States has, or after the war will have a financial interest, once Canada has paid for the particular developments to which the Minister of Munitions and Supply referred.

I shall reply first to my hon. friend's last question. The exchange of notes which have been tabled sets out the full basis of the arrangements made between the government regarding the development of the Canol project. Those were read into the record this afternoon and they show the means by which final disposition will be made.
There was a change made in the government's policy regarding airports.
If my hon. friend will please let me proceed, I am referring to the Canol project which is the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is the only item
before the committee.
The Alaska highway is also before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is the item before the committee:
Expenses of liaison officers in connection with the Alaska highway and Canol projects.

The hon. member for
Vancouver South is correct.

May I be permitted to
continue? My understanding is that the United States authorities who constructed the pipeline and refinery at Whitehorse can either operate them directly or arrange to have them operated by agents. When the war is over, the basis of settlement, the liquidation of the matter if you like, will be as is clearly set out in the exchange of notes. The Canol project is not in the same category as the airfields. The hon. member for Vancouver South referred to a statement made some little time ago by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. It is true that so far as the airfields are concerned the Canadian government is paying the United States government for the work done, because it represents assets which will be of permanent value to Canada. I think that answers the first part of my hon. friend's question.

What about the Alaska
highway?

The exchange of notes provided for the Alaska highway. So far as I am aware there has never been any suggestion that Canada should pay the United States for the expenditures on the Alaska highway. There were certain extensions to airfields which were found necessary and for which we will repay them.
With regard to the second to the last point raised by my hon. friend, he seemed to fear that we were giving Imperial Oil some sort of monopoly in the Northwest Territories and he inquired whether companies would have the right to go in there.
And individuals and syndicates.

I made a statement on
government policy on May 5 when the order in council setting forth the arrangements and giving the details of the proposed regulations was tabled. I should like to quote from that statement as reported on page 2651 of Hansard, as follows:
3288	COMMON'S
War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
In respect to the new regulations to ibe established, the order in council sets out briefly some of the more important conditions that will be imposed. It is to the general advantage of Canada that an active programme of exploration and search for oil should be carried out in order that new sources may be found and developed. The regulations will make available to all companies and individuals the opportunity of exploring and developing these resources.
The policy of the government with respect to the matter is set out in those words. There is no attempt to restrict this to any one company. As I have pointed out once or twice already in the discussion, the regulations provide that while the company can retain a permit of one area up to 2,000,000 acres, it must within a period of years reduce that and settle upon what particular acreage it is going to take. The limit of the acreage that it can have when it reaches that point is 350,000 acres.
What happens to the remainder?
It is open to anyone else. My hon. friend can go in and explore it.

Could I have all
;he rest?
If you stake it.	[DOT]

My hon. friend could go in; anyone else could go in. We were particularly careful in framing these regulations to provide against the very danger that the hon. member for Vancouver South has in mind. I have stated already that ultimately a pipeline must be built if the area, is to be commercially exploited, and that must be open to everyone upon terms approved by the government. I do not know how anything more could have been done to make certain that any company or individual that was interested should have an opportunity of going in and staking.
This is not a field of operations for an individual or company with small capital. You must transport your drilling equipment and supplies and everything else nearly 1,500 miles over very costly water and land transportation routes. You will have only three or four months in the summer for drilling operations and you must face heavy winter conditions. It is not a field for the small individual, such as Turner valley. This is not because of any limitation imposed by the government; it is because of limitations imposed by nature.
Is it a fact that the proven field has been reserved for Imperial Oil?

One-third or a little more of the proven field was covered by the old

leases which Imperial Oil obtained twenty years ago, the other two-thirds being secured under the war-time regulations. There is no doubt that the area is now under the control of Imperial Oil, but within a radius of fifty miles of Norman Wells there are over 5,000,000 acres.

How much more does
Imperial Oil control?
I am just coming to that. As I say, within a radius of fifty miles of the proven field there are over 5,000,000 acres, and of that Imperial Oil have a right to secure a permit covering 140,000 acres.
In addition they could get permits for over another million acres?

I suppose they could.
There is one other point I wish to mention. There is no doubt that at the moment Imperial Oil are in a position that may be regarded as advantageous compared with that of any other company coming in, but that is on account of the fact that they went in there twenty years ago and found oil. They were the people to whom the United States authorities went because they were on the spot and knew something about the country. It may be argued that they have a preferred position, but that preferred position may not be of any permanent value to them. I may add that other large oil companies are showing an interest in that country and, if they want to go in, they are free to go in. Perhaps I may just mention that while it is true that the pit-prop producers, when the $3.50 subsidy was withdrawn, were allowed to raise their own price by $3.50, when they tried to deliver their materials to the mines they were told by the mine owners, "We do not want your product, because we can buy it from the government at a lower figure." That in itself justifies the criticism which came from the Alberta Mine Timbers Retail association. They protested most vigorously against the use of this type of labour to produce a commodity which, by reason of the circumstances under which it is produced, can be sold at a lower price than regular producers can afford to charge.
While I recognize that the wartime prices and trade board and the Commodity Prices Stabilization corporation are tied in with this, it is sometimes extremely difficult, especially with the set-up as it is to-day, always to be in order when one discusses it, because there are three organizations involved-the two I have mentioned, and a government department. I object to any policy whereby the government puts prisoners of war and conscientious objectors at work to produce a commodity and thus undersell persons who are regularly engaged in that type of work. The minister suggested that that was not being done. I hope not, but we have reason to believe that it is.

Prisoners of war and
conscientious objectors come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour, and I

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
wish my hon. friend clearly to understand that at no time have they been used in competition with what may be termed free labour in an effort to undersell ordinary producers. That is an elementary and fundamental principle. My hon. friend can make any case he likes, but I assure him that under no circumstances is the product of prisoners of war and conscientious objectors underselling the products of free labour.

With reference to the employment of prisoners of war, what the Minister of Labour has said is quite true. The wages which are paid prisoners of war to-day by ' companies do not cheapen the production of what 'they create, and certainly in none of the companies by whom they are employed has civilian labour in any way been prejudiced. These people are used only where civilian labour is not sufficiently plentiful. I feel, however, that the scanty proportions of this vote reflect the government's policy toward forest services generally. The minister shakes his head, but we find that from year to year during the war the expenditure in his own department on this work has been less as the years go by. From 1939 to 1942 there has been a very substantial reduction.
I do not think that upon this item we should get into a general discussion in connection with forests.

This subject pertains to forest services generally, and the amount to be voted under this item has to do only with forest -services. I submit that considerable latitude has been taken even by the minister himself; we have been in Russia and Japan and all over the Pacific. We also took in a lot of latitude in the items which preceded this.

I think too much latitude has been taken under all these items. This particular one states definitely, "Internment and prisoners of war operations"; it does not have to do with general policy in connection with forests.
Very well, Mr. Chairman.

I wish to make one or two remarks in reply to the hon. member who has just spoken. He is under a misapprehension or perhaps in some confusion. This vote is not intended for forest development work; it is to provide for the supervisory expense of looking after certain internees or prisoners of war.
It is the first item under ""forest service".

Quite true. As I have explained, that is what this vote is for, but my hon. friend is under a misapprehension if he measures by this vote what we are doing in forestry work. In our civil estimates, which in due course will be before the house, is an item of over $300,000 for forestry work. But this has nothing to do with that; it is merely a vote for which we are asking to supervise the work of internees and prisoners of war who happen to be employed at dominion forest experimental stations.

The vote last year under this item was $42,445. Will the minister tell us what the actual expenditures were, and also what income accrued to the department through the sale of what these men produced?

I have already explained to the committee that the work of these internees and prisoners under supervision was directed to the production of cordwood, pit-props, a small amount of lumber, fence posts, and pulpwood.
Those were sold?

I can give my hon. friend the figures. There were produced over 16,000 cords of wood, including 5,000 cords to heat the internment camps; 2,750,000 odd lineal feet of mine props; over 12,000 lineal feet of fence posts, including fence posts for the internment camp; over 1,100 cords of pulp-wood; and over 55,000 feet board measure of sawn logs. My hon. friend asked what the receipts were. I am sorry we have not that here, but the material was sold at prices fixed by the timber fuel controller.

Item agreed to.
Forest products laboratories, $56,400.
Will the minister explain this item?

This is war work carried out by the laboratories. The purpose is to ascertain the best means of preservation and fire retardment treatment of wood for various purposes, serviceability of wooden aircraft under different climatic conditions, recovery of ethyl alcohol from wood waste for use in the manufacture of synthetic rubber, the use of paper plastics for aircraft and for other purposes, charcoal for producer gas and metallurgical pui poses, the moulding of aircraft parts to double curvature, the seasoning of lumber for special war purposes, and work of that kind. That is all directly related to the war.

How many different laboratories are there?
There is one in Montreal, one in Ottawa and one in Vancouver. That is the character of the work done, and the increase is due simply to the increasing demand made on laboratories by war services.

Some time ago there was a discussion about the possibility of setting up a forest products institute in Vancouver in connection with the university of British Columbia. I understand that a tentative agreement was reached between the dominion government, the provincial government and the board of governors at the university and the timber industry at the coast. What progress has been made with that project?

-Some discussions in that regard have gone on with the government of
British Columbia, with the university of British Columbia, and with the timber industry in that province, and I understand that substantial progress has been made. The likelihood is that before very long an agreement will be worked out.
When will that project be undertaken? Is it a post-war project?

It was agreed that it would be post-war, that it would be carried on after the war. It involves the erection of a building, and the provision of facilities and equipment necessary for the work. It would be difficult at the moment to get the labour and materials for the construction and equipment necessary.
But it is the intention to go ahead with it?

Yes. The agreement is
practically worked out and I have no doubt we shall cany it through. At least I hope so.
Is the general laboratory work carried on for post-war as well as for war purposes?
In Vancouver?
No, in the estimates?

Yes. It is directed mainly to war work now, but these are the functions carried on by the department in normal times. They have been carrying on research work and investigations but since the war most of the work has been directed to matters relating to the War.

I wish to emphasize again the scanty attention that has been paid by the dominion department to the forest products

industry. When one considers what has been done during war years in Germany and in other European countries, one sees that our amounts as well as our efforts are infinitesimal in comparison with the enormous resources we have to deal with. I know the minister does not want me to hold up the estimates, but this afternoon we discussed possible treaties with Russia and the question of how we are going to fight Japan, and what we shall do in the post-war period. Many hon. members on the other side of the house have emphasized the importance of the gold mining industry to give employment in the post-war days, and we can all agree with that.
Which was all out of order.

No. Mr. Chairman. I submit that the hon. member for Parry Sound was not out of order when he was dealing with gold mining under the minerals item. The minister himself now states that this is for post-war considerations as well. However, I realize that these are war appropriations and I will not hold them up long, though I submit again that this side of the house has not been doing all the holding up. Let me emphasize that our whole approach as a dominion parliament and as a dominion government to our post-war possibilities in the forest products industry, and to post-war employment that will be given by that industry, has been very much neglected. Indeed, it has been a miniature compared with the part that the forest products industry plays in the war and the part that it will play after the war. Just consider the different uses of the forest products of this country, from hospital waddings to the parcelling of goods for the boys overseas, buildings, wall board, as well as ammunition, and all sorts of paper requirements, the things that are used every day in the war. Consider the tremendous shortage that exists and the difficulty we are experiencing in maintaining the supply of pulps for explosives and waddings, pulps to make parcels, and so on. There is, I repeat, a vast shortage and this is a small vote for the laboratory work during war time. The time has come when as a dominion we must assume more of the responsibility for the promotion and encouragement of the second greatest industry in Canada, the one that offers the greatest possibilities in the post-war period, the industry that is second only to food production in the requirements of the war. The minister has mentioned $300,000 that may be brought down later. He says, I believe, that that is more than was spent in 1941 and 1942, when the expenditure was $60,000, less than in 1939. Well, $300,000 is

War Appropriation-Mines and Resources
not much for an industry that brings in, in revenue alone, almost SSO.OOO.OOO a year, an industry that pays out in wages $200,000,000, an industry that employs between 300,000 and 400,000, an industry that plays a more important part than any other except agriculture. It may be said that this comes under the provinces, in connection with civil and property rights. Well, one might just as well say the same about agriculture. We must realize that if we are to win the war and to win the peace that will follow we must have some practical and creative policies in our approach to a sound development of our great natural resources. Some would say, "Very well, we will handle all that through the state", but if we are to give employment to our people we must realize that we have a part in protecting, maintaining and preserving the great forest wealth of Canada that lies behind such employment.
I am not going to deal with many of the items on which the government might well spend money. The spruce bud-worm situation has been mentioned here. If the government were doing its duty toward our great natural resource it would have a larger vote directed toward the crucial years of the spruce bud-worm infestation, much larger than the amount mentioned here for all other laboratory purposes. I wish to mention only the general principle and the utter neglect which the government has shown toward this great industry not only in recent years but for many years. I am delighted to find that the leader of this party, Mr. John Bracken, who has studied the problems of this industry, as he has carefully studied the problems of other industries, made a speech not long ago in which he demonstrated his appreciation of the part our forest resources may play in post-war development. I urge the minister seriously not only to consider increasing this vote, but when he brings down his other estimates, not to talk about $300,000, but to assume the responsibility that he should towTard an industry that has been so long forgotten.
I realize that this item is not a large one. I am not criticizing it for its size; I am criticizing it because it is scanty and is an indication of the government's appreciation of the problem. In this dominion we have done practically nothing for the forest industry. The minister's department has spent more on the national parks of Canada alone than on the promotion of all the forest products of the country. When one stops to realize it, Mr. Chairman, one must think that if we have not awakened in peace times we should have awakened in war time, and for war purposes we should at least
be abreast of other nations who have been spending not in one year but for twenty years amounts that make us look like a backward nation. We are a nation that holds the key to the greatest forest resources development of any nation in the world. I urge the minister to reconsider, especially when he is bringing down his other estimates, increasing the vote in order to do the many things that are waiting to be done. I urge that he increase his other vote and give forestry its proper place in this country.
I may say here that after the next election- and it may not be long in coming; it is well indicated now-we shall have a keener appreciation of the forestry industry and we are likely to have a forestry department. In the meantime the minister who has had a long experience in the mines department, may at least take a leaf out of the constructive book of Mr. Bracken and show some progressive productivity.
Where is he?

He is out studying the problems that hon. members who have just made that remark do not understand, and I am glad that we see the results of some of that study in a clear comprehension of the problems that confront this country.

The boundless optimism of my hon. friend as to what may happen in the next election certainly challenges one's admiration. He chides us for the smallness of this vote. He criticizes the government because of its parsimony in dealing with the problems of the forest wealth of this country, and he evinces a remarkably keen interest-

-a newly discovered interest in pushing forward the value of our timber assets. I said, "All governments in the country"; I did not confine it only to this government.
My hon. friend did not say that.
Yes, I did; I said "all governments".
My hon. friend directed his shafts at this government.
I said "all governments".

If you go back to the days prior to the Conservative regime of 1930, that started in those unfortunate early years of 1930, what do you find the government of the day, the Liberal government, did? Look at the records and see what it was spending on work of this kind and contrast it with, I was almost going to say the parsimony of my hon. friend's party when it was in power from 1930 to 1935. Contrast that again with what has been done from 1935 up to the present time, even during the last five years of war. Why, my hon. friend has not a single peg on which to hang his hat.
That is why we need a new interest now; we have a new day coming.

The new interest that would be provided by my hon. friend would be a retrograde interest. I would be desperately afraid if the thing were entrusted to my hon. friend. However, this vote does not cover what the department is doing for the development of forest resources; it is merely for the supervision of the work of these prisoners of war in internment camps.

Prince Rupert-Terrace^Cedarvale highway, $3,000,000.

Would the minister giye a break-down of this item? Would he also
explain why the federal government, after starting a highway which when completed was to extend from Vancouver to Prince Rupert, should leave a small portion of eighteen miles for the provincial government to complete? The people of British Columbia, and particularly those of the Prince Rupert district, are rather incensed at the federal government for leaving that small portion to be completed by the province. Would the minister explain this item and why that work is being left to the province?

It will be necessary to deal very briefly with the genesis of this road. Ordinarily, as the hon. member for New Westminster knows, the dominion government does not go into a province and build a road. Years ago, under the government of the present Prime Minister, we did build what is known as the Big Bend highway in British Columbia. The road under discussion never would have been undertaken by the federal government if it had not been for the needs of war. The suggestion for the road came first, I believe, from the United States chiefs of staff; it was concurred in by the Canadian chiefs of staff, and was recommended by the permanent joint board on defence. Its origin is similar to that of the Alaska highway, the development of the Canol project which we were discussing this afternoon, and other matters. In considering the defence of North America the military authorities had to keep constantly in mind the possibility that coastal traffic would be interrupted. At a certain period of the war that was a danger. There was a road of sorts, capable of supporting truck traffic, from Vancouver to Hazelton, on the old Grand Trunk Pacific.
A road of sorts.

Parts of it were all right; parts perhaps were not so good. At any rate it was a passable road. There was also a road of sorts from Hazelton toward Terrace, which under certain weather conditions was capable of being used by vehicles. Between Cedarvale and Prince Rupert, for a distance of ninety-seven miles, there was no road whatever. That country was a wilderness; the only outlet was the old Grand Trunk Pacific railway. It is not my place or my function to pass judgment upon the opinions held by military people, but certainly the chiefs of staff at Washington, supported by the chiefs of staff in Canada and the permanent joint defence board, recommended the construction of this road from Terrace to Prince Rupert in order to provide an alternative route in case

the railroad should be destroyed. This was predicated, perhaps, on a very long chance that coastal communications might be interrupted.
The chance was not so long at one time.	'

Perhaps not; I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South that there was a definite possibility. That is why the road was undertaken. Nothing was known about the country, so that reconnaissance surveys had to be run. The work was entrusted to the Department of Mines and Resources, and under the surveys and engineering branch, in charge of Mr. Wardle, these surveys were made as speedily as possible. Undoubtedly greater difficulties intervened than had been expected. Surveys had to be made. There was a good deal of rock work, and much heavy timber to be moved. There was difficulty in getting labour and in getting materials. There were unfavourable climatic conditions, all of which increased the cost of the road, and delayed its construction very considerably beyond the period at which it was hoped it would be completed.
The fortunes of war have changed. If conditions at the beginning of 1942 had been as they are to-day, the probability is that the road would not have been recommended. It was built as insurance, and was thoroughly justified on that ground.
Why not complete it?
I shall deal with that. The road was not constructed as an ordinary provincial road. The building of roads within provinces is the function and responsibility of the provinces.
Not all roads.

Yes, all roads, with the exception of the transcontinental highway, where the federal government has assumed certain responsibilities. But this road was constructed for military purposes. That military need has disappeared.
Not necessarily.
Well, the military need, in the opinion of the chiefs of staff, has, I think pretty well disappeared.
Sometimes they have been wrong.

The road, in addition to the original section from Terrace to Prince Rupert, has an additional mileage from Terrace to Kitwanga. That was also included in the construction. It is expected that the total cost will be between $10,000,000 and $11,000,000.
TMr. Crerar.]

I am of opinion, and I am sure that the chiefs of staff recommended that this road should be completed-
Well, now-
-because it was necessary.

Finish, not extend.

No; the demand is that the road should be built further by the federal government. The whole matter was carefully considered by the government. In this appropriation we have $3,000,000 to complete some sections of the road which were not completed, and for maintenance purposes during the year.
Now, what the province gets out of it is 110 miles of a good and completed road, with bridges.

What does the
dominion get out of it?
The dominion gets-
Security.
Well, yes, it gets security, which was indicated in the first instance. But I say now-
Is the war over?
I say now to the committee that I do not think the road would have been undertaken, in the light of conditions as they exist to-day.

The same applies to the Alaska
highway.
Of course.

The extension between
